readme.text: # mdsf Format, and lint, markdown code snippets using your favorite tools. ## Table of contents - [Table of contents](#table-of-contents) - [Installation](#installation) - [Linux & MacOS](#linux--macos) - [Windows](#windows) - [Cargo](#cargo) - [npm/npx](#npmnpx) - [Homebrew](#homebrew) - [Conda](#conda) - [Usage](#usage) - [Formatting code](#formatting-code) - [Caching formatting results](#caching-formatting-results) - [Removing old caches](#removing-old-caches) - [Verifying code](#verifying-code) - [GitHub Action](#github-action) - [Visual Studio Code](#visual-studio-code) - [Vim / NeoVim](#vim--neovim) - [conform.nvim](#conformnvim) - [treefmt](#treefmt) - [pre-commit](#pre-commit) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Language aliases](#language-aliases) - [Newlines](#newlines) - [Custom tools and commands](#custom-tools-and-commands) - [Tools](#tools) - [Commands](#commands) - [Shell completions](#shell-completions) - [Bash](#bash) - [Zsh](#zsh) - [Fish](#fish) - [PowerShell](#powershell) - [Elvish](#elvish) - [Nushell](#nushell) - [Rust MSRV](#rust-msrv) - [Acknowledgement](#acknowledgement) - [Alternatives to mdsf](#alternatives-to-mdsf) ## Installation The latest version of `mdsf` can be downloaded directly from [github.com/hougesen/mdsf/releases](https://github.com/hougesen/mdsf/releases). ### Linux & MacOS ```shell curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/hougesen/mdsf/releases/latest/download/mdsf-installer.sh | sh ``` ### Windows ```powershell powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://github.com/hougesen/mdsf/releases/latest/download/mdsf-installer.ps1 | iex" ``` ### Cargo Install using the [published crate](https://crates.io/crates/mdsf): ```shell cargo install mdsf --locked ``` or directly from source: ```shell git clone git@github.com:hougesen/mdsf.git cargo install --path ./mdsf --bin mdsf ``` If you do not have Cargo installed, you need to [install it first](https://www.rust-lang.org/learn/get-started). ### npm/npx You can install `mdsf` using [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mdsf-cli): ```shell npm install -g mdsf-cli mdsf format . ``` or run it directly using npx: ```shell npx mdsf-cli format . ``` ### Homebrew ```shell brew install hougesen/tap/mdsf ``` ### Conda An _unofficial_ (and unsupported) Conda package can be found at [https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/mdsf](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/mdsf). ```shell conda install conda-forge::mdsf ``` ## Usage ``` mdsf 0.12.0-next Format, and lint, markdown code snippets using your favorite tools Mads Hougesen Usage: mdsf [OPTIONS] Commands: format Run tools on input files verify Verify files are formatted init Create a new mdsf config completions Generate shell completion cache-prune Remove caches help Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s) Options: --log-level [default: debug] [possible values: trace, debug, info, warn, error, off] -h, --help Print help -V, --version Print version ``` ### Formatting code The `format` command, as the name implies, is used to format documents. ```shell mdsf format file.md ``` ``` Run tools on input files Usage: mdsf format [OPTIONS] [INPUT]... Arguments: [INPUT]... Path to files and/or directories Options: --stdin Read input from stdin and write output to stdout --config Path to config file --debug Log stdout and stderr of formatters --threads Amount of threads to use. Defaults to 0 (auto). --cache Cache results --log-level [default: debug] [possible values: trace, debug, info, warn, error, off] --timeout Tool timeout in seconds. Defaults to no timeout. --on-missing-language-definition What to do when a codeblock language has no tools defined. Falls back to the value defined in your config file, if no argument is provided. [possible values: ignore, fail, fail-fast] --on-missing-tool-binary What to do when the binary of a tool cannot be found. Falls back to the value defined in your config file, if no argument is provided. [possible values: ignore, fail, fail-fast] -h, --help Print help (see a summary with '-h') -V, --version Print version ``` #### Caching formatting results To speed formatting caching can be enabled by supplying the `format` command with the `--cache` argument. ```shell mdsf format --cache docs/ ``` ##### Removing old caches Old caches can be removed by running the `mdsf cache-prune` command. ``` Remove caches Usage: mdsf cache-prune [OPTIONS] Options: --log-level [default: debug] [possible values: trace, debug, info, warn, error, off] -h, --help Print help -V, --version Print version ``` ### Verifying code You can verify that the document is formatted using the `mdsf verify` command. ```shell mdsf verify docs/ ``` ``` Verify files are formatted Usage: mdsf verify [OPTIONS] [INPUT]... Arguments: [INPUT]... Path to files and/or directories Options: --stdin Read input from stdin and write output to stdout --config Path to config file --debug Log stdout and stderr of formatters --threads Amount of threads to use. Defaults to 0 (auto). --timeout Tool timeout in seconds. Defaults to no timeout. --log-level [default: debug] [possible values: trace, debug, info, warn, error, off] --on-missing-language-definition What to do when a codeblock language has no tools defined. Falls back to the value defined in your config file, if no argument is provided. [possible values: ignore, fail, fail-fast] --on-missing-tool-binary What to do when the binary of a tool cannot be found. Falls back to the value defined in your config file, if no argument is provided. [possible values: ignore, fail, fail-fast] -h, --help Print help (see a summary with '-h') -V, --version Print version ``` ### GitHub Action There are a lot of different ways to run `mdsf` using GitHub actions. The easiest way, in my opinion, is to use the official GitHub action to install mdsf. After that you can run the binary like you would in your terminal. > \[!NOTE\] > mdsf is not a package manager. > > You must also install the tools you wish to use in your GitHub action. ```yaml name: mdsf on: push jobs: format: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout repository uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Install mdsf uses: hougesen/mdsf@main - name: Run mdsf run: mdsf format --log-level warn . - name: Commit changes uses: EndBug/add-and-commit@v9 with: message: "style: formatted markdown code blocks" ``` ### Visual Studio Code [![](https://img.shields.io/visual-studio-marketplace/v/hougesen.mdsf?color=374151&label=Visual%20Studio%20Marketplace&labelColor=000&logo=visual-studio-code&logoColor=0098FF)](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=hougesen.mdsf) [![](https://img.shields.io/visual-studio-marketplace/v/hougesen.mdsf?color=374151&label=Open%20VSX%20Registry&labelColor=000&logo=data:image/svg+xml;base64,&logoColor=0098FF)](https://open-vsx.org/extension/hougesen/mdsf) mdsf can be run using the VSCode extension. > \[!NOTE\] > The mdsf VS Code extension does currently not support installing mdsf. > Which means mdsf must be installed using other means. ### Vim / NeoVim #### conform.nvim [conform.nvim](https://github.com/stevearc/conform.nvim) has native support for running mdsf. ```lua local conform = require("conform") conform.setup({ formatters_by_ft = { markdown = { "mdsf" }, -- ... }, -- ... }) ``` ### treefmt Add the following to your `treefmt.toml` to run mdsf using [treefmt](https://github.com/numtide/treefmt). ```toml # treefmt.toml [formatter.mdsf] command = "mdsf" options = ["format"] includes = ["*.md"] ``` ### pre-commit See [pre-commit](https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit) for instructions Sample `.pre-commit-config.yaml`: ```yaml repos: - repo: https://github.com/hougesen/mdsf rev: main hooks: - id: mdsf-format ``` ## Configuration The default configuration of `mdsf` aims to as simple as possible. For that reason the default formatter for each language is the one most people have installed. If you are interested in customizing which formatter is run, you can create a new `mdsf` configuration file by running `mdsf init`. ``` Create a new mdsf config Usage: mdsf init [OPTIONS] Options: --force Create config even if one already exists in current directory --format [default: json] [possible values: json, toml, yaml] --schema-version [default: locked] [possible values: locked, stable, development] --log-level [default: debug] [possible values: trace, debug, info, warn, error, off] -h, --help Print help -V, --version Print version ``` `mdsf` supports running multiple formatters on the code snippet. ```json { "languages": { // Only run `ruff` on Python snippets, "python": "ruff:format", // Run `usort` on file and then `black` "python": ["usort", "black"], // Run `usort`, if that fails run `isort`, finally run `black` "python": [["usort", "isort"], "black"], // Formatters listed under "*" will be run on any snippet. "*": ["typos"], // Formatters listed under "_" will only be run when there is not formatter configured for the file type OR globally ("*"). "_": "prettier" } } ``` ### Language aliases Multiple languages can easily be mapped to the same tools using the `language_aliases` option. ```json { "language_aliases": { "language": "is_alias_of" } } ``` In the example below `bash` and `zsh` would use the tools defined under `languages.shell`. ```json { "languages": { "shell": "shfmt" }, "language_aliases": { "bash": "shell", "zsh": "sh

repo_cards.description: Catch API bugs before your users do

readme.text:
## Schemathesis > **Catch API bugs before your users do.** Schemathesis automatically generates thousands of test cases from your OpenAPI or GraphQL schema and finds edge cases that break your API.


Finding bugs that manual testing missed

## Try it now ```console # Test a demo API - finds real bugs in 30 seconds uvx schemathesis run https://example.schemathesis.io/openapi.json # Test your own API uvx schemathesis run https://your-api.com/openapi.json ``` ## What problems does it solve? - 💥 **500 errors** that crash your API on edge case inputs - 📋 **Schema violations** where your API returns different data than documented - 🚪 **Validation bypasses** where invalid data gets accepted - 🔗 **Integration failures** when responses don't match client expectations - 🔄 **Stateful bugs** where operations work individually but fail in realistic workflows > ⚠️ **Upgrading from older versions?** Check our [Migration Guide](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/blob/master/MIGRATION.md) for key changes. # Installation & Usage **Command Line:** ```console uv pip install schemathesis schemathesis run https://your-api.com/openapi.json ``` **Python Tests:** ```python import schemathesis schema = schemathesis.openapi.from_url("https://your-api.com/openapi.json") @schema.parametrize() def test_api(case): # Tests with random data, edge cases, and invalid inputs case.call_and_validate() # Stateful testing: Tests workflows like: create user -> get user -> delete user APIWorkflow = schema.as_state_machine() # Creates a test class for pytest/unittest TestAPI = APIWorkflow.TestCase ``` **CI/CD:** ```yaml - uses: schemathesis/action@v3 with: schema: "https://your-api.com/openapi.json" ``` ## Who uses it Used by teams at **[Spotify](https://github.com/backstage/backstage)**, **[WordPress](https://github.com/WordPress/openverse)**, **JetBrains**, **Red Hat**, and dozens of other companies. > "_Schemathesis is the best tool for fuzz testing of REST APIs on the market. We at Red Hat use it for examining our applications in functional and integration testing levels._" - Dmitry Misharov, RedHat ## See it in action 🔬 **[Live Benchmarks](https://workbench.schemathesis.io)** showing continuous testing results from real-world APIs: - Code & API schema coverage achieved - Issues found with detailed categorization - Performance across different fuzzing strategies ## Reporting - **[Allure](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/guides/allure/)** — Rich visual reports with per-operation results, failure steps, and curl reproduction commands - **[JUnit XML](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/guides/cicd/)** — For GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, and any CI tool that consumes JUnit ## Documentation 📚 **[Documentation](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/)** with guides, examples, and API reference. ## Get Help - 💬 [Discord community](https://discord.gg/R9ASRAmHnA) - 🐛 [GitHub issues](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/issues) ## Contributing We welcome contributions! See our [contributing guidelines](CONTRIBUTING.md) and join discussions in [issues](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/issues) or [Discord](https://discord.gg/R9ASRAmHnA). ## Acknowledgements Schemathesis is built on top of Hypothesis, a powerful property-based testing library for Python. ## License This project is licensed under the terms of the [MIT license](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT).

items.name: Release 4.17.0
items.body_excerpt:
### :rocket: Added

- Capture path-parameter values from successful 2xx requests for reuse during fuzzing.
- Capture request-body field values from successful 2xx requests for reuse during fuzzing.
- Coverage phase records request identifiers into the runtime resource pool for reuse in later phases.
- Use identifiers from the runtime resource pool for resource-bound parameters and body fields during the coverage phase.
- Use captured body-field values to fill resource-bound fields in the examples phase.
- Enable the runtime resource pool for producers that return empty response bodies.
- Chain `st fuzz` scenarios via inferred and schema Links, biased 80% toward link-driven steps.
- Pick correlated identifiers for nested-resource operations during the coverage phase.
- Dependency inference recognizes `<resource>Name`-style body fields on collection paths (e.g. `POST /products {productName: ...}`).
- Dependency inference recognizes more identifier-style path parameters (e.g. `username`, `containerGroupName`).
- Dependency inference treats `POST /resource/{name}` as a producer when the response has no body.
- Dependency inference treats `POST /collection {idField: ...}` as a producer when the response has no body.
- Dependency inference recognizes `GET /collection` returning an array of identifier strings.
- Dependency inference recognizes plural `{ids}` path parameters (e.g. `GET /persons/{ids}`).
- Seed the runtime resource pool with identifier values from a Bearer JWT or HTTP Basic username.

### :bug: Fixed

- False positive `negative_data_rejection` for body-level type mutations on `multipart/form-data` endpoints. [#3801](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/issues/3801)
- False positive `negative_data_rejection` for body fields with `format: binary` or `format: byte`.
- Crash on schemas with non-schema values inside `properties` (e.g. an integer where a sub-schema is expected).
- Cascading generation failures after one schema corrupted shared `hypothesis

items.name: Release 4.16.0
items.body_excerpt:
### :rocket: Added

- `schemathesis.openapi.require_security_scheme()` for scoping auth providers to specific OpenAPI security schemes. [#3745](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/issues/3745)

### :bug: Fixed

- Query parameters not serialized when `style`/`explode` are omitted from the spec, ignoring OpenAPI 3.0 defaults.
- Use the matching registered serializer for multipart fields with `encoding.contentType`. [#3785](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/issues/3785)
- `before_call` hook setting a missing required header in the coverage phase had no effect. [#3784](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/issues/3784)
- Request timeouts reported as a check failure when a replay made them flaky.

#### `positive_data_acceptance` false positives

- *`example` values violating constraints (examples phase):*
  - When an object schema-level `example` has a property violating a nested `format` constraint (e.g. `date-time` without timezone).
  - When a parameter-level `example` value violates its declared schema type.
  - When a schema-level parameter `example` violates the parameter's own constraints (e.g. `pattern`).
  - When a response-derived parameter example violates the parameter's schema constraints.
  - When a response-derived parameter example violates the parameter's `format` constraint.
  - When a property `example` violates its field's own type (also applies to the coverage phase).
  - For content-encoded header parameters with object examples.
  - For property examples violating `anyOf`/`oneOf` constraints via bundled `$ref`s.
  - For array body properties with `minItems` > 1 and object items.
  - When assembled body violates the schema (e.g. `allOf` with `additionalProperties: false`).
  - When a required property has an unsatisfiable schema.

- *Composition (`allOf` / `oneOf` / `anyOf` / `$ref`) in the coverage phase:*
  - For `oneOf` branches with nested multi-`$ref` `allOf`.
  - For `oneOf` body schemas where generated values satis

scout.summary: mdsf is an active Rust-based CLI tool for formatting code blocks in Markdown using a wide range of external linters and formatters. It offers flexible installation methods, extensive editor/tooling integrations, and frequent feature releases expanding supported tools and configuration options.
highlights: Supports installation via shell script, PowerShell, Cargo, npm/npx, Homebrew, and Conda [E-RD-004, E-RD-005, E-RD-006, E-RD-007].
Recent releases (v0.11.0–v0.12.0) rapidly expand supported tools (e.g., swiftlint, kube-linter, oxfmt) and add TOML/YAML config support [E-RL-001, E-RL-002, E-RL-003].
Well-integrated with development ecosystems: GitHub Actions, pre-commit, VS Code, Vim/Neovim, treefmt [E-RD-002].
Project shows healthy maintenance with CI badges (GitHub Actions, Codecov), changelog, and contribution guidelines [E-RD-001, E-RF-001].
risks: Conda package is explicitly marked as unofficial and unsupported, which may confuse users seeking stable distribution channels [E-RD-007].
High velocity of new tool integrations may impact stability or testing coverage, though CI and release notes suggest active quality control.

inventor.summary: mdsf is a Rust-based CLI tool that enables formatting and linting of code blocks within Markdown documents by delegating to external tools, with recent innovations in configuration flexibility and extensibility.
highlights: Introduces support for defining configuration files in TOML and YAML formats, enhancing usability and integration [E-RL-001].
Enables users to define custom tools and commands, significantly expanding adaptability beyond built-in formatters [E-RL-003].
Rapidly incorporates new language/tool support (e.g., swiftlint, kube-linter, oxfmt), demonstrating an extensible architecture [E-RL-001, E-RL-002].
Provides multi-platform installation scripts (shell, PowerShell) and integrates with package managers like Cargo, npm, Homebrew, and Conda [E-RD-004, E-RD-005, E-RD-006, E-RD-007].
risks: The ability to define arbitrary custom tools may introduce security or stability risks if users execute untrusted commands [E-RL-003].
Unofficial Conda distribution lacks project support, potentially leading to inconsistent user experiences or outdated versions [E-RD-007].

engineer.summary: mdsf is a well-structured Rust CLI tool that delegates Markdown code block formatting to external linters/formatters, with strong extensibility, multi-platform support, and active maintenance.
highlights: Built in Rust with clear project structure including Cargo.toml, rust-toolchain.toml, and rustfmt.toml, indicating disciplined language/toolchain management [E-RF-001].
Supports flexible configuration via TOML/YAML and custom tool definitions, enabling broad adaptability across languages and workflows [E-RL-001, E-RL-003].
Provides robust installation options (shell, PowerShell, Cargo, npm, Homebrew) and editor integrations (VS Code, Vim/Neovim), enhancing developer experience [E-RD-004, E-RD-005, E-RD-006, E-RD-002].
Maintains CI/CD hygiene with GitHub Actions, Codecov, pre-commit hooks, and regular dependency updates visible in release notes [E-RD-001, E-RF-001, E-RL-001, E-RL-002, E-RL-003].
risks: Custom tool execution capability introduces potential for unsafe command injection if user-supplied configurations are not properly sandboxed [E-RL-003].
Reliance on unofficial Conda package may lead to version skew or lack of support for users depending on that distribution channel [E-RD-007].

skeptic.summary: While mdsf presents itself as a versatile and actively developed tool, several claims about stability, support, and security warrant caution.
highlights: The project advertises broad tooling support and frequent releases, but the rapid addition of new formatters (e.g., kube-linter, swiftlint) may outpace thorough testing or documentation [E-RL-001, E-RL-002].
Installation methods include direct execution of remote scripts via curl and PowerShell, which poses inherent security risks if the delivery channel is compromised [E-RD-004, E-RD-005].
Configuration extensibility allows custom tool definitions, but without clear sandboxing or validation, this could enable arbitrary code execution [E-RL-003].
The Conda package is explicitly labeled 'unofficial' and 'unsupported,' yet it's listed alongside first-party installation methods, potentially misleading users about its reliability [E-RD-007].
risks: Blind trust in remote install scripts (shell/PowerShell) introduces supply-chain attack vectors [E-RD-004, E-RD-005].
Custom tool execution feature lacks evident safeguards against command injection or unsafe binaries [E-RL-003].
Unofficial distribution channels (Conda) may lag behind or diverge from official releases, creating inconsistency and support confusion [E-RD-007].
Despite CI badges and release notes, the low number of forks (5) and modest stars (106) suggest limited community scrutiny for a tool handling code execution [E-RD-001, repo_profile].

scout.summary: The aquaproj/aqua repository is an active Go-based CLI version manager with notable adoption by several companies and projects. It emphasizes declarative tool management, lazy installation, registry-based ecosystems, and automated updates via Renovate. The project maintains a clean root structure, provides documentation, and has recent releases, though some release notes are empty.
highlights: Used by multiple well-known companies including Mercari, DeNA, Gunosy, and Retty [ID:E-RD-006].
Supports key features like per-project version switching, team-wide tool standardization, lazy install, and secure operations [ID:E-RD-003].
Integrated with Renovate for continuous dependency updates, evidenced by an open Dependency Dashboard issue [ID:E-IS-001].
Project documentation is available online and linked in README; includes contribution guidelines and logo assets [ID:E-RD-002], [ID:E-RF-001].
Recent patch release (v2.57.2) includes bug fixes and deprecations, showing active maintenance [ID:E-RL-003].
risks: Two recent releases (v2.58.0-0 and v2.58.0-1) have empty release notes, reducing transparency for users [ID:E-RL-001], [ID:E-RL-002].
High number of open issues (173) relative to forks (62) may indicate unresolved bugs or feature requests [repo_profile].

inventor.summary: aqua is a declarative CLI version manager that enables per-project tool versioning, team-wide standardization, and secure lazy installation through a registry-based ecosystem, with automation support via Renovate.
highlights: Enables switching CLI tool versions per project and unifying installations across teams and CI [ID:E-RD-003].
Features lazy installation and a registry-driven ecosystem for extensible tool management [ID:E-RD-003].
Supports continuous updates through Renovate, evidenced by an active Dependency Dashboard [ID:E-IS-001].
Adopted by multiple engineering organizations including Mercari, DeNA, Gunosy, and Retty [ID:E-RD-006].
Recent patch release (v2.57.2) fixed jar support, architecture mapping, and checksum parsing issues [ID:E-RL-003].
risks: Two latest releases (v2.58.0-0 and v2.58.0-1) lack release notes, hindering user awareness of changes [ID:E-RL-001], [ID:E-RL-002].
High open issue count (173) may indicate unresolved technical debt or scalability challenges [repo_profile].

engineer.summary: aqua is a Go-based declarative CLI version manager that supports per-project tool versioning, lazy installation, and registry-driven tool management, with active maintenance and adoption by multiple engineering teams. It integrates with Renovate for automated updates and provides secure, standardized tool provisioning across teams and CI environments.
highlights: Core features include per-project CLI version switching, team-wide tool standardization, lazy install, and registry-based extensibility [ID:E-RD-003].
Actively maintained with recent patch fixes for jar support, architecture mapping (x86-64 → amd64), and checksum file parsing [ID:E-RL-003].
Used in production by notable companies including Mercari, DeNA, Gunosy, Retty, and Masterpoint Consulting [ID:E-RD-006].
Automated dependency updates via Renovate, confirmed by an open Dependency Dashboard issue [ID:E-IS-001].
Project structure includes standard Go tooling files (go.mod, go.sum), CI/CD configs (.goreleaser.yml, renovate.json5), and documentation assets [ID:E-RF-001].
risks: Latest two releases (v2.58.0-0 and v2.58.0-1) have empty release notes, reducing visibility into changes or potential breaking updates [ID:E-RL-001], [ID:E-RL-002].
High open issue count (173) relative to community size may indicate unresolved bugs or scalability limitations [repo_profile].

skeptic.summary: While aqua presents itself as a robust CLI version manager with enterprise adoption and active maintenance, several red flags undermine confidence in its reliability and transparency, including missing release notes for recent versions, a high volume of unresolved issues, and potentially overstated claims about security and ecosystem maturity.
highlights: Claims of 'Secure' operation [ID:E-RD-003] lack supporting evidence such as audit reports, SBOMs, or detailed security practices beyond a Security Scorecard badge [ID:E-RD-002].
Adoption by major companies [ID:E-RD-006] is cited anecdotally via blog posts and discussions, but no verifiable integration depth or production-scale validation is provided.
Lazy Install and Registry features [ID:E-RD-003] sound compelling but are not explained technically—raising questions about trust model, supply chain risks, and failure modes.

scout.summary: Schemathesis is an active, well-maintained Python tool for automated API testing that leverages OpenAPI and GraphQL schemas to generate test cases, detect bugs, and enforce contract compliance. It supports advanced features like stateful testing, fuzzing with captured values, and security scheme scoping, with recent releases enhancing coverage and fixing critical serialization and hook issues.

inventor.summary: Schemathesis is an innovative API testing tool that invents realistic, state-aware test scenarios by leveraging schema definitions and runtime feedback to uncover deep integration and edge-case bugs.
highlights: Invents test cases by automatically generating thousands of inputs from OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas, including invalid and edge-case data [E-RD-002].
Introduces a runtime resource pool that captures successful response values (e.g., IDs, names) and reuses them in subsequent requests to enable realistic, stateful test sequences [E-RL-001].
Pioneers link-driven test chaining—using OpenAPI Links or inferred relationships—with 80% bias toward valid workflow transitions, simulating real user journeys [E-RL-001].
Detects subtle contract violations like schema mismatches, validation bypasses, and stateful failures that traditional testing misses [E-RD-005].
Extends fuzzing intelligence by recognizing resource-bound fields (e.g., `productName`) and populating them with captured or correlated identifiers during coverage and examples phases [E-RL-001].
risks: Advanced test generation logic (e.g., link chaining, resource pooling) may produce complex or non-deterministic test flows that are hard to debug without detailed tracing [E-RL-001].
Heavy reliance on schema accuracy means incomplete or incorrect OpenAPI specs could limit test effectiveness or generate misleading results [E-RD-002, E-RD-005].

engineer.summary: Schemathesis is a robust, actively developed Python-based API testing framework that leverages OpenAPI and GraphQL schemas to generate comprehensive, state-aware test cases. It integrates fuzzing, property-based testing, and runtime feedback to expose critical bugs like 500 errors, schema violations, and workflow failures, with strong CLI and pytest support.
highlights: Generates thousands of test cases from OpenAPI/GraphQL specs, including edge cases and invalid inputs, to uncover hidden bugs [E-RD-002].
Uses a runtime resource pool to capture and reuse successful response values (e.g., IDs, body fields) across test phases, enabling realistic stateful testing [E-RL-001].
Implements intelligent test chaining via OpenAPI Links or inferred relationships, with 80% bias toward valid sequences, improving integration test fidelity [E-RL-001].

skeptic.summary: While Schemathesis claims to automatically find deep API bugs through advanced test generation and stateful chaining, its effectiveness hinges on schema completeness and may overpromise on real-world reliability given recent bug fixes and complex, potentially flaky workflows.
highlights: Claims of finding 'real bugs in 30 seconds' [E-RD-004] and uncovering issues 'manual testing missed' [E-RD-003] lack independent validation or reproducible benchmarks.
Heavy reliance on OpenAPI/GraphQL schema accuracy means incomplete or incorrect specs could severely limit test coverage or produce false positives/negatives [E-RD-002, E-RD-005].

Recent releases still fix critical issues like auth mismatches [E-RL-002], parameter serialization defaults [E-RL-003], and hook ineffectiveness [E-RL-003], suggesting instability in core functionality.
risks: Stateful test chaining with 80% bias toward link-driven steps [E-RL-001] may create unrealistic or non-reproducible workflows that mask true failure modes or introduce flakiness.
Runtime resource pooling and inferred correlations (e.g., `productName`) [E-RL-001] could propagate incorrect assumptions if initial requests succeed by chance, leading to misleading test passes.
Migration warnings [E-RD-006] combined with frequent feature additions and bug fixes indicate a rapidly evolving codebase where backward compatibility and long-term reliability are uncertain.
